title: Page Eleven
subtitle: Wednesday to Saturday: a Witness Nobody Wants Alive, a Seed Salesman from St. Louis, and Whose Names Go to Court

setting.name: Kansas City, Wednesday 4 to Saturday 7 November 1936
setting.description: The reckoning. The machine has won, and now it is tidying up. Big Sid Varnum has decided that Virgil Strode, who knows everything and is visibly coming apart, must cease to be a problem, and that the book, which carries his nephew's initials, must cease to exist. He has wired St. Louis for a professional, who checks into the Muehlebach on Thursday as a seed salesman. Strode, who has worked out what he is worth, wants to trade himself and the book to the federal government for his life. Special Agent Merriwether wants the book and the witness and, more than he admits, the convictions. Horace Quarterman wants the book burned. The Monitor wants a headline, and has one drafted. Judge Orville Stanfield wants Lt. Voyles in his courtroom on Friday afternoon to explain the merry-go-round under oath. And the party, holding the book or knowing who does, has four days to decide whose names in it go to court: the rich men at the back, the poor men in the middle, or the dead at the front.
setting.atmosphere: After the holiday, the hangover. Torn bunting in the gutters, sample ballots blowing down Main Street, the radio back to dance bands and grain prices, the first snow flurries on Friday. Downtown is marble and hush: the Federal Building, the Muehlebach lobby, Varnum Bonding's frosted glass. Eighteenth Street is getting on with its life and is angry, quietly, everywhere: in the barbershop, in the pews, on the bandstand. The Lincoln Arms is warm and full of musicians passing through. The tone is the end of a hard-boiled paperback: fewer fights and harder ones, conversations where every sentence costs something, and a choice at the end that nobody can make for the players.

keyLocations.name: The Hotel Savoy, Room 612, and the Lincoln Arms
keyLocations.description: The Savoy is an old downtown hotel of dark wood and stained glass, faded and respectable, where Virgil Strode has lived alone since his wife died in 1931. Room 612: a bed, a desk, a radio, a phonograph and a shelf of records he bought on Eighteenth Street, his wife's photograph. The Lincoln Arms on Eighteenth Street is where no white man in Kansas City would think to look for another, and where any white stranger who walks into the lobby is noticed by everyone in it within ten seconds.
features: Room 612's phonograph and records: race records from the Eighteenth Street shops, a whole shelf, played until they are grey
The Savoy's lobby, bellhops and switchboard; its service stairs; its fire doors
The Lincoln Arms' third floor, rooms 3A to 3F, the musicians' floor, where Jules lives, a ballroom's worth of witnesses
Mr. Garfield Oates at the Lincoln Arms desk, who was paid five dollars to forget two white men once and will not be again
encounters: The Savoy's night bellhop, Mr. Dewitt Earle, Black, sixty, who has carried Strode's bags for five years and likes him
Mr. Everett Brumley (The Professional), from Thursday night
secrets: CLUE H4 (core, if the party meets Strode on Wednesday on his terms, somewhere he believes is safe, and promises him protection): he names Norbert Varnum as the man who brought the cash, seven times since June, $11,400, and signed for it with his initials in Strode's book 'because Sid wanted a record of who was paid and Norbert is too stupid to know it was a record of who paid'. He names Voyles as the man who 'handled' Fry ('I did not know. I swear before God I did not know until Wednesday'). He names Gleason, the precinct captains in the Second and Fourth Wards and the Health Department clerk. He says that the machine's ghosts in the white wards are in another book, which Norbert keeps, and that he has never seen it.

Strode's price: immunity from Merriwether, in writing, and to be alive. He also, and this surprises him as much as anyone, asks the party for one more thing: that the names of the dead in his book be struck from the rolls 'before anyone uses them again'. He knew what he was doing. He did it anyway. He would like, now, to have done one decent thing.

Moving Strode to the Lincoln Arms is the best protection in the city, and the party should be allowed to think of it. Nobody downtown would look for him there, and a white stranger asking for him in that lobby would be the most conspicuous man in Kansas City. It is also a lot to ask of Eighteenth Street: the man who stole its dead, sleeping on its third floor. Jules, Geneva, Mr. Oates and the musicians must agree, and the conversation in which they do (or do not) is one of the campaign's great scenes. Jules may say yes for reasons of his own: 'I want him alive. I want him alive in a courtroom saying my mother's name.'

keyLocations.name: The Muehlebach and Varnum Bonding
keyLocations.description: The Muehlebach Hotel: twelve storeys, marble, the machine's guests and the visiting governors, a Black workforce of bellmen, porters, maids and waiters and no Black guests. Varnum Bonding and Surety on Main Street: two storeys of plain brick, a waiting room of men in hats, an inner office of mahogany, a safe, and the files. Big Sid sees petitioners every morning from nine to eleven.
features: The Muehlebach register at the front desk, and the bell captain, Mr. Silas Worthy, who knows every guest's habits because his men carry them
Varnum Bonding's waiting room: a radiator, a spittoon, twelve chairs and a picture of the President
Norbert Varnum's office: a glass partition, an adding machine, and a filing cabinet of carbon copies
Big Sid's office: mahogany, a cane in a stand, no papers on the desk ever
encounters: Big Sid Varnum (Mob Boss), who will see the party if they ask; it is his custom to see everyone
Mr. Silas Worthy, bell captain at the Muehlebach
Mr. Everett Brumley, reading a seed catalogue in the Muehlebach lobby
secrets: CLUE H2 (core, from Rudy Spurlock, a Lincoln High boy who carries telegrams for Western Union at night, if anyone on Eighteenth Street asks who carried for Varnum Bonding on Wednesday): at 10 a.m. Wednesday, a wire from Varnum Bonding to a St. Louis address, a pool hall on Market Street: 'NEED SEED SALESMAN THURSDAY STOP USUAL TERMS STOP N.V.' Rudy remembers because the boss's own nephew signed it and tipped a nickel.

CLUE H3 (core, from Mr. Worthy or any Muehlebach bellman, through the hotel's Black staff, who see everything and are asked nothing; a Black party member asking in the staff corridor gets it free, a white one asking at the front desk gets nothing): 'E. Brumley, St. Louis, seed and nursery supplies', registered Thursday 2 p.m., room 1011, paid in advance by Varnum Bonding's account. He went out at four and asked the doorman the way to the Savoy, 'to see an old friend'. He carries a sample case that is too heavy for seeds.

CLUE H5 (core, for anyone who gets into Norbert's filing cabinet: a night burglary of Varnum Bonding, Heat +2, Mechanics or Sleight of Hand DC 15 for the lock; or Norbert himself, frightened enough): carbon copies of seven Midland Merchants Bank slips: cash withdrawals from a Varnum Bonding 'campaign fund' account on the same seven dates and in the same amounts as the back pages of Strode's book, each signed N. Varnum. With the book, this is the case against the top.

Big Sid, if the party goes to see him: he is courteous, unhurried and frightening. He offers, for the book, $5,000 cash, the Gold Leaf's liquor licence for life, every charge dropped (Saturday's river road, the river-bluff bodies if any, Lem Castle's suspension lifted), and his word. He does not mention Strode at all. If the party mentions Strode, he says 'Virgil has resigned. He was very tired.' If the party refuses, he thanks them for their time and has his secretary show them out. He never threatens. Insight DC 14: he has already decided what happens to the party if they refuse, and he is in no hurry.

keyLocations.name: The Federal Building and the Monitor
keyLocations.description: Agent Merriwether's borrowed desk on the fifth floor, and down the hall the office of an assistant United States attorney who has never tried an election case. Two miles away on Grand Avenue, the Kansas City Monitor, the reform evening paper: a city room of typewriters and smoke, a managing editor named Russell Kearns who has been fighting the machine for nine years and losing.
features: Merriwether's file, now a box: the 1934 election, the Burnham Hotel, and whatever the party has given him
The Monitor city room, the composing room, and a front page for Friday already in proof: GHOST VOTE IN NEGRO WARDS: DEAD CAST HUNDREDS OF BALLOTS ON EIGHTEENTH STREET
encounters: Mr. Russell Kearns, managing editor of the Monitor, crusading, impatient and blind in one particular direction
Mr. Kenneth Lowe, the assistant U.S. attorney, who wants a case he can win
secrets: Merriwether and Lowe, given the book, will prosecute. Without Strode alive to explain the back pages, and without H5, the case is what they can see: ghost votes in the Second and Fourth Wards, the precinct captains whose names are on pages 1 to 74, the floater drivers on page 79, a few repeaters, Ogden Fry (dead). Lowe says, frankly, that the drivers 'are the easiest convictions in the book'. Merriwether, if the party argues with him, can be brought to see what that would mean. If the party gives him Strode, H4, H5 and Mrs. Whitaker, he can reach Norbert Varnum, Gleason and Voyles, and he says so; Big Sid himself, he says, 'will take years'.

Kearns's headline: he has a tip from somebody at the Board (in fact from Norbert Varnum, on his uncle's instructions) that the ghost vote was 'a colored precinct racket'. It suits the machine perfectly and suits Kearns's crusade too: it is a story. If Beatrice Albright is played and has the book, the photographs and Mrs. Whitaker's list, she can force the true story onto the front page: the ghosts are Black, the hands that voted them were white and paid from Main Street, and the living were turned away. Persuasion DC 15, or automatic if she has both F3 photographs and H1; she may have to threaten to take it to the Black weekly instead, which would print it gladly and which Kearns would never forgive.

If nobody stops it, the headline runs Friday evening, and on Saturday morning Horace Quarterman is on the courthouse steps telling reporters that Eighteenth Street has been slandered, which is true, and that the book should be burned, which is not.

keyLocations.name: Judge Stanfield's Courtroom
keyLocations.description: Friday at 2 p.m. Judge Orville Stanfield has summoned Lt. Conrad Voyles to explain under oath why a prisoner named in a writ of habeas corpus was released at 3 a.m. into the custody of persons unknown, and why the prisoner's booking cards bear three different names. Hezekiah Wilburn appears for Julius Ransom. The courtroom is public. Eighteenth Street fills the gallery.
features: The witness box, walnut, with a carved eagle on it
The gallery, standing room only, Rev. Pettus in the front row
The press table: the Monitor, the Black weekly, and a wire-service man who smells a story
encounters: Lt. Conrad Voyles and a machine lawyer
secrets: Voyles under oath: he lies smoothly about the merry-go-round ('clerical errors at three stations') and the release ('the prisoner asked to leave'). The party can break him with evidence: A3 (the trusty), A5 (the cards in one hand), the release order from the spike, Jules's own testimony, Dr. Mayhew's medical evidence, and, if they have it, Patrolman Kavanagh, who will testify about Precinct 14 if asked by someone he trusts. E-clues about Fry, put to him in open court, make Judge Stanfield refer the matter to the grand jury. Voyles is not arrested on Friday. He is finished, and he knows it, and that makes him more dangerous on Friday night.

If Lem Castle was suspended, Hezekiah Wilburn can ask Judge Stanfield, as a matter arising, to inquire into the suspension of an officer who acted to prevent a murder; Judge Stanfield cannot order the department, but he can say what he thinks from the bench in front of the press, and Captain Darrow quietly reinstates Lem on Monday.

Mrs. Whitaker, if she is in the gallery and her notebook is safe, can be called by Wilburn on a related matter and asked to read her count into the record. It is not strictly relevant to a writ. Judge Stanfield allows it.

synopsis: Wednesday: Virgil Strode, given a resignation to sign, meets the party in a place he thinks is safe and offers them what he has: Norbert Varnum's cash, Voyles's handling of Fry, Gleason, the captains, everything, for immunity from the federal government and his life, and one more thing he did not expect to ask for: that the names of the dead be struck from the rolls. Varnum Bonding wires a pool hall in St. Louis for a 'seed salesman'. On Thursday the professional, Mr. Everett Brumley, checks into the Muehlebach, asks the doorman the way to the Savoy, and begins to watch room 612. Big Sid Varnum, visited, offers $5,000, the Gold Leaf's licence for life and every charge dropped, for the book. Agent Merriwether wants it for a case that, as the assistant U.S. attorney cheerfully admits, will be easiest against the floater drivers and the Black precinct captains. Horace Quarterman wants it burned. The Monitor has a Friday front page in proof that says GHOST VOTE IN NEGRO WARDS. The party may move Strode to the one place no one would look for him, the musicians' floor of the Lincoln Arms on Eighteenth Street, if Eighteenth Street will have him. On Friday afternoon Judge Stanfield puts Lt. Voyles in the witness box over the merry-go-round, and the gallery is full; on Friday night, with the first snow falling, Brumley and a ruined Voyles both come for Strode and the book. On Saturday the party decides where the book goes and whose names in it go to court. The campaign ends on Saturday night at the Gold Leaf, with the band, and with whatever has become true.
hook: Wednesday 4 November 1936, seven in the morning. The sample ballots are blowing down Eighteenth Street like leaves, and Mr. Dandridge is sweeping the shop back into a barbershop. On the desk upstairs is the card from last night: Hotel Savoy, room 612. At 7:15 the barbershop telephone rings, and Mr. Dandridge calls up the stairs that it is a white man asking for 'the people from the Gold Leaf', and that he sounds like he has not slept. 'They have asked me to resign,' says Virgil Strode, when someone takes the receiver. 'The letter is already typed. It is dated today. I would like to talk to you somewhere with a great many people in it.'

conclusions.conclusion: H. Big Sid has sent for a professional, and the money in the book leads to his nephew
clues: H1: the back pages of the book, 'recd. of N.V.' (the book)
H2: the wire to St. Louis, carried by Rudy Spurlock (Western Union)
H3: the Muehlebach register and the sample case (the bell captain)
H4: Strode's own account (wherever he is safe)

conclusions.conclusion: Brumley will kill Strode on Friday night and burn the book
clues: Brumley asks the Muehlebach doorman the way to the Savoy, and the Savoy's bellhop Dewitt Earle about room 612 (Thursday)
Brumley buys a can of lighter fluid and a pair of rubber gloves at a drugstore on Main Street, seen by a porter (Friday morning)
Brumley pays for his room through Saturday morning only and has a ticket on the 11:50 p.m. Friday train to St. Louis (the Muehlebach desk, Union Station)
Quarterman: 'Sid's man came in on the noon train Thursday. They always do it the night before they leave.'

conclusions.conclusion: Voyles can be broken in open court
clues: A3 and A5: the trusty's plates and the booking cards in one hand
The release order from Number Two's spike
Jules's testimony and Dr. Mayhew's medical evidence
E1 to E4 about Fry, put to him on the stand
Patrolman Kavanagh, if asked by someone he trusts

acts.title: Act 1: Room 612
acts.description: Wednesday. Strode's call. The meeting (somewhere with a great many people in it: Union Station's waiting room, the Liberty Memorial's steps at noon, the Gold Leaf at lunch) and H4. The decision where to keep him. Rudy Spurlock and the wire (H2). The book's destination begins to be argued over: Merriwether, Quarterman, the Monitor, each with their case. By Wednesday night the party should have Strode safe somewhere, know a professional is coming, and know that every party with an interest in the book has a reason that sounds good.
objectives: Hear Strode's offer and decide whether to protect him
Find a place to keep him that the machine will not think of
Learn that Varnum has sent for someone
Hear Merriwether's, Quarterman's and the Monitor's cases for the book

scenes.name: Under the Clock
scenes.description: Strode meets the party wherever they choose; if they let him choose, it is the great waiting room at Union Station, under the clock, at ten. He gives H4 if he believes the party will protect him. He is precise, frightened, and honest for the first time in years. He says that the white wards' ghosts are in another book, Norbert's, that he has never seen. He asks for immunity, his life, and, unexpectedly, the names of the dead struck from the rolls. If anyone from Eighteenth Street is with the party, he finds it very hard to look at them, and does anyway.
scenes.readAloud: Under the great clock in the waiting room at Union Station, with a thousand people walking past and the trains being called to Chicago and St. Louis and Denver in a voice like a cathedral, Virgil Strode sits on a long oak bench with his hat on his knees and his camel coat buttoned to the neck. He looks as if he has not slept since Sunday, which is true. When you sit down beside him he does not turn his head. 'Seven times since June,' he says, to the clock. 'Eleven thousand four hundred dollars. Norbert brought it in an envelope from the Midland Merchants Bank and initialled my book, because Sid likes a record of who has been paid, and Norbert has never understood that it is also a record of who paid.' A train is called. He waits for it to finish. 'I should like to be alive at Christmas. And I should like those names taken off the rolls. Both, if it can be managed. I am aware that I am in no position to ask for the second.'

skillChecks.success: Every word is true, and he has held nothing back except his shame, which he is holding very tightly. He did not know about Fry until Wednesday. He will testify.
skillChecks.failure: He seems sincere. You cannot be sure. He gives H4 anyway, because he has nowhere else to go.

skillChecks.success: He agrees to go where the party puts him, without asking where, and to stay there until Saturday. He gives the party the key to room 612, and says that his wife's photograph is in the desk drawer and he would like it if anything happens.
skillChecks.failure: He insists on going back to the Savoy for his things tonight. It is a risk the party must manage.

scenes.name: The Third Floor
scenes.description: If the party proposes the Lincoln Arms: Jules, Geneva, Mr. Oates and the musicians on the third floor must agree to hide Virgil Strode, the man who stole their dead, for three nights. Run it as a conversation, not a check. Jules's position: 'I want him alive. I want him in a courtroom saying my mother's name.' Geneva's: 'If they find him here, they burn this hotel.' Lucky's: he will stand outside Strode's door all night, and he will not speak to him. Mr. Oates: 'I took five dollars once to forget two white men. I'd like to remember one.' Strode himself, brought up the back stairs, stands in the corridor and does not know where to put his hands. If they agree, Strode is in room 3F, and a white stranger asking for him in the lobby is the most noticed man in Kansas City. If they refuse, that is their right, and the party must find another place (Rev. Pettus's church basement; the Albright house on Ward Parkway, if Beatrice dares; Merriwether's custody, which leaks).
scenes.readAloud: The third-floor corridor of the Lincoln Arms is narrow and warm and smells of hair oil and coffee and valve oil, and someone in 3B is practising a trumpet with a mute, the same four bars over and over. Jules Ransom is leaning in his doorway with his right arm still strapped to his ribs, and Geneva beside him with her arms folded, and at the end of the corridor, very large, Lucky Bowden is sitting on a kitchen chair with his hands on his knees. The trumpet stops. Everyone on the floor has come to their door. Virgil Strode stands at the top of the back stairs in his camel coat with his hat in both hands, and for a long moment nobody says anything at all.

skillChecks.success: The floor agrees, on terms: Strode stays in 3F, he does not come down, he does not speak to anyone he is not spoken to by, and on Saturday he goes to court. Jules shakes on it. Strode, astonished, thanks them, and Geneva says 'Don't.'
skillChecks.failure: The floor agrees for one night only. On Thursday the party must find somewhere else, or ask again with something better than an argument.

skillChecks.success: Jules is doing this for his mother, and for himself, and it is costing him more than he shows. Later, alone, he asks the party whether they think a man like Strode can be sorry. Do not answer for them.
skillChecks.failure: Jules says yes very calmly. You do not see what it costs.

scenes.name: Three Cases for a Book
scenes.description: In whatever order the party meets them on Wednesday and Thursday: Merriwether (and Lowe), Quarterman, and Kearns of the Monitor, each with a case for the book. Merriwether: 'Give it to the government and it goes to court.' Lowe, beside him, cheerfully: 'The drivers are the easiest convictions in the book.' Quarterman: 'Burn it, and my people don't go to prison for Big Sid.' Kearns, with Friday's front page in proof: 'GHOST VOTE IN NEGRO WARDS. Give me the book and I'll name every name.' Each is partly right. Let the players argue with each of them, and win some ground with each, and lose some.
scenes.readAloud: Russell Kearns has the front page in proof on his desk, still damp, and he turns it round so you can read it upside down: GHOST VOTE IN NEGRO WARDS, in type an inch high. 'Nine years,' he says. 'Nine years I've been trying to hang this machine and this is the first time I've had a rope. A tip from inside the Board, and if you've got what I think you've got, the names.' He lights a cigarette from the one he is finishing. 'I don't care who it embarrasses. That's the point of a newspaper.' He does not seem to notice that he has just said exactly what the man who gave him the tip wanted him to say.

skillChecks.success: Kearns, shown the book's pages 75 to 80 (the crews from the Burnham Hotel) and the back pages, and Mrs. Whitaker's list: he pulls the headline. He wants the true story instead, and he will print it if he can be given the photographs and the back pages. If Beatrice is played, this is her scene, and she gets the byline.
skillChecks.failure: Kearns will think about it. Without more, the headline runs on Friday.

skillChecks.success: Merriwether, pressed about the drivers: he had not thought about it, and it troubles him. He says that if he has Strode alive and the deposit carbons, he can 'go up the ladder instead of down it', and that he will put it in writing that the drivers and repeaters are witnesses, not defendants, if he has Strode.
skillChecks.failure: Merriwether says the law is the law, and does not see the trap yet.

skillChecks.success: Quarterman, met as an equal and with respect: he concedes that burning the book also burns the only proof that Eighteenth Street was robbed, not robbing. He will not help the federal government. He will, if the drivers are protected, stay out of the way, and he will tell the party when Sid's man came in ('noon train Thursday; they always do it the night before they leave').
skillChecks.failure: Quarterman says he has survived twelve years by not trusting white men's promises and is not going to start with a federal one.

encounters: No fights expected on Wednesday. If Strode insists on going back to the Savoy alone on Wednesday night, two of Gleason's men are watching the lobby (Street Tough x2), and he needs an escort

acts.title: Act 2: The Seed Salesman
acts.description: Thursday. Brumley arrives on the noon train and registers at the Muehlebach (H3). Big Sid receives the party, if they go to see him, and makes his offer. Norbert Varnum can be frightened or burgled (H5). Brumley walks to the Savoy and asks about room 612, and begins to look for Strode; if Strode is at the Lincoln Arms, Brumley has to come to Eighteenth Street, where he is the most conspicuous man in the city, and he knows it. By Thursday night the party should know who Brumley is, what he is for, and roughly when.
objectives: Identify the professional and where he is staying
Hear Big Sid's offer, and answer it
Get the deposit carbons, or Norbert

scenes.name: Nine to Eleven
scenes.description: Big Sid's morning hours at Varnum Bonding. The waiting room is full of men in hats who want a job, a licence, a bond, a brother out of jail. The party is called in out of turn. Big Sid makes his offer: $5,000, the Gold Leaf's licence for life, every charge dropped, Lem Castle's suspension lifted, and his word. He never mentions Strode. He never threatens. He asks, politely, after Jules's health. If the party refuses, he thanks them. Norbert stands behind his right shoulder throughout and does not speak.
scenes.readAloud: The inner office is mahogany and leather and absolutely bare: no papers on the desk, no photographs, only a blotter, a silver inkstand that has never been used and a black cane in a brass stand by the window. Big Sid Varnum does not get up. He is heavy and bald and quiet, and his small eyes move from one of you to the next and stop on each exactly as long as it takes to put a price on them. 'I like to see people,' he says. 'Every morning, nine to eleven, I see anybody who comes. A man who can't be seen can't be trusted.' He folds his hands. 'You have something of mine. I'd like to buy it. I'd like everybody to go home happy. How does five thousand dollars sound, and Mrs. Templeton's licence for as long as she lives, and nobody ever hearing about Saturday night again?'

skillChecks.success: He has already decided what happens to the party if they refuse, and he is in no hurry about it. He has also, in the last five minutes, decided that Norbert is a liability, because Norbert flinched when the book was mentioned. Norbert can be turned, and Big Sid has just given you the lever.
skillChecks.failure: He is a reasonable businessman making a reasonable offer. That is the most frightening thing about him.

skillChecks.success: You let him believe you are considering it, and agree to meet his man on Saturday at noon at the Liberty Memorial with 'the item'. It buys a day: Big Sid tells Brumley to concentrate on Strode and leave the book for Saturday.
skillChecks.failure: He smiles and says, 'Take all the time you need,' which means none.

scenes.name: The Staff Corridor
scenes.description: The Muehlebach: H3 from the bell captain Mr. Silas Worthy and his men, who carry every bag and see everything and are asked nothing. A Black party member who goes in by the staff entrance and asks in the corridor gets it all for a cigarette and a straight answer; a white party member at the front desk gets a polite refusal. This is the color line turned around: the people the hotel pretends not to see are the ones who know. Mr. Worthy adds that the seed salesman's sample case is too heavy for seeds and that he asked the doorman the way to the Savoy.
scenes.readAloud: The staff corridor of the Muehlebach runs behind the grand lobby like the inside of a wall: bare bulbs, painted brick, a time clock, a trolley of breakfast trays and a smell of coffee and floor polish, and a dozen Black men in maroon-and-gold uniforms sitting on a bench under a sign that says NO SMOKING, smoking. The bell captain is a tall grey man with a waxed moustache and white gloves folded over his belt, and he hears you out without a word, and looks at the others on the bench, and then back at you. 'Ten-eleven,' he says. 'Mr. Brumley. Seeds. Came in on the noon train with a sample case two of my boys had to carry between them.' He smooths his moustache. 'Nobody ever asks us anything. We could tell them what every man in this building had for breakfast and who he was with when he ate it.'

skillChecks.success: Mr. Worthy adds that Brumley paid through Saturday morning only, and that the bell desk has his ticket on the 11:50 p.m. Friday train to St. Louis waiting to be collected. Whatever he is here to do, he means to do it Friday night.
skillChecks.failure: You get room 1011 and the name. The rest the party can work out from the desk or from Quarterman.

skillChecks.success: Room 1011 while Brumley is out (Mr. Worthy's pass key, if he trusts the party): the sample case holds a .45 automatic, a sound-deadening sleeve for it that a gunsmith made, rubber gloves, a can of lighter fluid, a Savoy room-service jacket, and a photograph of Strode from the Monitor. Nothing else. No seeds.
skillChecks.failure: Brumley comes back early. Getting out of the room needs a bellman's help or a fire stair, and Brumley now knows someone has been in. He moves faster.

scenes.name: Norbert
scenes.description: Norbert Varnum, forty, soft and anxious, who has just watched his uncle decide he is a liability. He can be frightened (Intimidation DC 14), reasoned with (Persuasion DC 15, easier if the party shows him the back pages of the book with his initials), or burgled (Varnum Bonding at night: Mechanics or Sleight of Hand DC 15, Heat +2). Either way, H5: the carbons of seven Midland Merchants Bank withdrawals matching the book. If he is reasoned with, he does more: he says that Big Sid told him on Wednesday to 'tidy up', and that he knows what that means because it is what his uncle said in 1934. He wants to go to Merriwether too. He is much less useful than Strode and much more frightened.
scenes.readAloud: Norbert Varnum has his coat on and his hat in his hand and is trying to leave by the back door of Varnum Bonding at six o'clock when you find him, and when he sees you he puts the hat on and takes it off again. He is forty and looks like a boy who has been sent to the principal. His fountain pen has leaked into the breast pocket of his good suit and he has not noticed. 'I only carried it,' he says, before anyone has asked him anything. 'I only carried the envelopes. Uncle Sid said initial them. I always initial things. I'm the treasurer.'

skillChecks.success: Norbert gives you the carbons from his own office and agrees to go to Merriwether. He also gives you the existence of the second book: the white wards' ghosts, in his safe, which he will open for the federal government and nobody else.
skillChecks.failure: Norbert panics, says he will deny everything, and runs. He is on the 11:50 train to St. Louis on Friday unless someone stops him, and his uncle knows he ran.

skillChecks.success: He gives you the carbons there in the alley, from his briefcase, and begs you not to tell his uncle. He will not testify.
skillChecks.failure: He screams for the night watchman, a Night Watchman with a whistle and a dog. Heat +1.

encounters: Varnum Bonding's night watchman and his dog (Night Watchman, Guard Dog), if the party burgles it
Gleason's men (Street Tough x2) shadowing the party after the visit to Big Sid

acts.title: Act 3: Snow on Eighteenth Street
acts.description: Friday. At 2 p.m. Judge Stanfield's courtroom: Voyles in the witness box, the gallery full, the merry-go-round and Fry put to him under oath. He is finished, and knows it. That evening the first snow. At 10 p.m. Brumley makes his move for Strode, wherever he is, in a Savoy room-service jacket if Strode is at the Savoy, or on foot on Eighteenth Street if he is at the Lincoln Arms. Voyles, with nothing left to lose, comes separately with Kreutz, for the book. Saturday morning: where the book goes. Saturday night: the Gold Leaf, the band, and whatever has become true.
objectives: Keep Strode alive through Friday night
Decide where the book goes, and whose names in it go to court
Get Lavinia Ransom's name off the register

scenes.name: Under Oath
scenes.description: Judge Stanfield's courtroom at 2 p.m. Hezekiah Wilburn examines; the party supplies the evidence and the witnesses. Voyles lies smoothly about clerical errors and a prisoner who asked to leave. Then the trusty Clifton Bynum, the booking cards, the release order, Dr. Mayhew on Jules's injuries, Jules himself, and (if the party has it) the Fry evidence and Patrolman Kavanagh. When it is done Judge Stanfield says from the bench that he is referring the testimony of Lieutenant Voyles to the grand jury, and the gallery stands up. Voyles walks out past Eighteenth Street in the corridor and looks at nobody.
scenes.readAloud: The gallery is Eighteenth Street in its Sunday clothes: Rev. Pettus in the front row with his hat on his knees, Mrs. Whitaker beside him with her handbag, Mr. Dandridge in a stiff collar, Willa Templeton, Zora in her new coat, the band in a row at the back, and standing along the wall, because there are no more seats, a hundred more. In the witness box, under the carved eagle, Lieutenant Conrad Voyles has his hands folded on the rail, one of them still bandaged, and is explaining in a soft, reasonable voice how a prisoner may come to be booked under three names in three stations through no fault of anyone at all. Judge Stanfield is listening with his chin on his fist. When Voyles has finished, the judge looks at the gallery for a long moment, and then at Hezekiah Wilburn. 'Mr. Wilburn,' he says. 'I believe you have a witness named Bynum.'

skillChecks.success: The party's witnesses, prepared and calm, tell it straight and the judge believes them. Voyles is referred to the grand jury for perjury and for the death of Ogden Fry.
skillChecks.failure: The witnesses are nervous and the machine's lawyer rattles one of them. Judge Stanfield refers Voyles for perjury only. It is still the end of him, more slowly.

skillChecks.success: Watching Voyles leave: he is not going home. He has nothing left to protect but himself, and the only thing that can still hang him is a living Strode and the book. He will come tonight.
skillChecks.failure: Voyles walks out looking calm. He is not.

scenes.name: The Most Conspicuous Man in Kansas City
scenes.description: Friday, 10 p.m., snow falling. If Strode is at the Savoy: Brumley comes up the service stairs in a room-service jacket with a tray and the silenced .45 under the napkin; the bellhop Dewitt Earle, who likes Strode, may warn the party if he has been asked to. If Strode is at the Lincoln Arms: Brumley has had to find out where he is (from Gleason's men, from a leak in Merriwether's office, or from following someone careless), and walks up Eighteenth Street in the snow in a grey overcoat, and every person on the street watches him go by, and by the time he reaches the Lincoln Arms lobby the third floor knows. He is a professional and he adapts: he tries the back stairs, the fire escape, the kitchen. Separately, Voyles and Kreutz, with nothing left, come for the book wherever the party keeps it. Brumley is the most dangerous single enemy in the campaign; Voyles is the most desperate. They are not working together; they may get in each other's way. Lucky Bowden is outside 3F on his kitchen chair.
scenes.readAloud: The snow has come in the evening, the first of the year, big soft flakes falling straight down through the light of the Gold Leaf's sign so that Eighteenth Street looks like a stage set, and it has emptied the street of everybody except the people who live on it, who are standing in their doorways watching it fall. Which is why everybody sees him. A white man in a grey overcoat and a grey hat, carrying nothing, walking east up the middle of the sidewalk with the snow settling on his shoulders, not hurrying, looking at the numbers on the doors. Mr. Dandridge sees him from the barbershop. Tadpole sees him from the Gold Leaf's doorway and is gone, running, before the man has passed the shoeshine stand. By the time the man in the grey overcoat reaches the steps of the Lincoln Arms, there are faces at every window on the street, and somewhere upstairs a trumpet that has been practising the same four bars all day has stopped.

skillChecks.success: You spot Brumley's approach (or the room-service jacket that does not fit) with a round to spare. The party chooses the ground: a narrow corridor, a stairwell, a dark kitchen.
skillChecks.failure: The first you know is a soft cough of a silenced pistol and Lucky Bowden's chair going over. Lucky is at 0 hit points and dying; Brumley is in the corridor.

skillChecks.success: With Brumley cornered and a dozen witnesses at their doors, you persuade him that the job is over: Strode's statement is already in a federal agent's hands and his death would hang Big Sid, not save him. Brumley, a professional, considers this, lays down the .45, and asks if he can still make the 11:50 to St. Louis. Whether he does is the party's choice.
skillChecks.failure: Brumley does not negotiate with people who have not yet shown him they can win. It is a fight.

skillChecks.success: Whoever Brumley shot lives: a Patch Job or steady hands in a hotel corridor in the snow-light, with Geneva holding the lamp. Dr. Mayhew, if played, has done this before on Eighteenth Street on worse nights.
skillChecks.failure: They need Wheatley-Provident tonight, and the ambulance must be called, and the police will come with it.

scenes.name: Page Eleven
scenes.description: Saturday morning. The party decides where the book goes. Options, any combination: to Merriwether, with Strode alive, H4, H5, Norbert if turned, Mrs. Whitaker's list and the party's insistence that the drivers and repeaters are witnesses, not defendants (the best outcome, and Merriwether will put it in writing); to the Monitor, with the true story and the photographs, under Beatrice's byline or not; to Quarterman, to burn (the drivers and captains are safe; the machine is safe; Eighteenth Street's dead stay on the rolls); to Big Sid at the Liberty Memorial at noon for $5,000 (the party is rich and Heat never falls below 3 again); or cut: pages 75 to 80 torn out to protect the drivers, which protects Amos Fairley and weakens the case against Gleason. Then, at Judge Stanfield's chambers at eleven, Hezekiah Wilburn and Mrs. Whitaker petition for the names of the dead to be struck from the rolls of Precinct 14, with Rev. Pettus's burial book as the evidence. Judge Stanfield signs it. Mr. Dandridge takes the register out of his window with a razor blade, very carefully, and gives Lavinia Ransom's line to Jules. The campaign ends on Saturday night at the Gold Leaf: the band, Jules at the piano with his ribs strapped, Geneva leaving for Chicago on Thursday, and 'Woodland Avenue' played all the way through.
scenes.readAloud: Mr. Dandridge takes the register out of his window himself, with a razor blade from the drawer, working the old paste loose from the glass a quarter-inch at a time so that the paper does not tear, and the morning light comes into the barbershop clear for the first time in a month. When the long sheets are free he lays them on the counter and runs his finger down the second column until he finds the line, and cuts it out, a strip of paper two inches long, and holds it out to Jules Ransom without a word. Ransom, Lavinia M., 1712 Woodland Ave. Jules looks at it for a long time. Then he folds it once and puts it in his breast pocket, behind his handkerchief, and says, 'Thank you, Mr. Dandridge,' and goes across the street to the Gold Leaf, where the band is waiting, and in a little while, through the open door, you hear him start to play.

skillChecks.success: Merriwether and Lowe put it in writing: the floater drivers, the repeaters and the Black precinct captains who testify are witnesses, not defendants; the case goes up the ladder to Norbert Varnum, Harvey Gleason and Lt. Voyles. Big Sid 'will take years'. Amos Fairley is safe.
skillChecks.failure: Merriwether promises, but not in writing, and Lowe is not in the room. The party has to decide whether to trust a federal promise, which is exactly what Quarterman warned them about.

skillChecks.success: The petition to strike the dead from the rolls, drawn by Wilburn with Rev. Pettus's burial book and the Health Department's own certificates: Judge Stanfield signs it for all 1,108 names in the Second and Fourth Wards. The dead of Eighteenth Street are off the rolls by Christmas.
skillChecks.failure: The petition is granted for Precinct 14 only, the 263 names the party proved. It is enough for Lavinia Ransom. The rest will take another year and another lawyer.

encounters: Mr. Everett Brumley (The Professional), Friday 10 p.m., at the Savoy or on Eighteenth Street
Lt. Conrad Voyles (Bent Detective) and Det. Sgt. Emil Kreutz (Crooked Cop), Friday night, for the book, wherever it is kept

If the party meets Big Sid's man at the Liberty Memorial on Saturday noon: a Mob Lieutenant and two Bodyguards, and an envelope of $5,000, and no trick, because Big Sid keeps his bargains, which is how he stays in business

npcsInvolved.name: Virgil Strode, 47
npcsInvolved.role: The book's author; now the witness
npcsInvolved.description: Narrow, balding, a camel coat buttoned to the neck, a shelf of Eighteenth Street records played grey. Precise, frightened, honest at last.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be alive at Christmas, and, to his own surprise, to have done one decent thing: the names off the rolls.

npcsInvolved.name: Mr. Everett Brumley
npcsInvolved.description: Colourless, courteous, a grey suit and a grey overcoat, a seed catalogue, a sample case too heavy for seeds. Use The Professional. Never angry, never in a hurry, never in a town longer than two nights.

npcsInvolved.name: Sidney 'Big Sid' Varnum, 63
npcsInvolved.description: Heavy, bald, small eyes, a bare mahogany desk, a cane. Sees everybody nine to eleven. Never threatens. Use Mob Boss.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Tidiness. The book gone, Strode gone, Norbert quiet, and the machine untouched.

npcsInvolved.name: Norbert Varnum, 40
npcsInvolved.description: Soft, frightened, a leaking fountain pen. Initials everything.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Not to be the next man his uncle tidies.

npcsInvolved.name: Special Agent Thomas Merriwether, 34
npcsInvolved.description: As before; this is the scenario where he has to choose between the case he can win and the case that is true.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A real case. Whether it is a just one depends on the party.

npcsInvolved.name: Russell Kearns, 50
npcsInvolved.description: Rolled sleeves, chain smoker, nine years of crusading and losing, and a headline in proof he is very proud of.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To hang the machine in print, by whatever rope he is handed.

npcsInvolved.name: Mr. Silas Worthy, 58
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, grey, waxed moustache, white gloves folded over his belt. Knows what every guest had for breakfast.

npcsInvolved.name: Lt. Conrad Voyles, 51
npcsInvolved.description: As before, until Friday at 2 p.m. After that, a man with nothing left to protect.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The book, and Strode dead, because they are the last things that can hang him.

rewards.money: If the party gave the book to the government or the Monitor, nobody pays them; Willa Templeton gives each of them a lifetime table at the Gold Leaf, and the band plays at any of their weddings for nothing. Merriwether can arrange a $200 federal informant's payment for the party as a whole, which they may take. Big Sid's $5,000, if they took it, is in an envelope, and is real.
items: Strode's statement, signed (Clue H4), and Norbert's deposit carbons (Clue H5)
Merriwether's letter, if they got it in writing: the drivers and repeaters are witnesses, not defendants
Judge Stanfield's order striking the dead from the rolls of Precinct 14, or of the Second and Fourth Wards
Lavinia Ransom's line from the register, which belongs to Jules
Brumley's .45 automatic, if taken; a professional's weapon, with a gunsmith's sleeve that the GM may rule makes it quiet
A lifetime table at the Gold Leaf

twists: The man who stole the names of the dead of Eighteenth Street can only be kept alive by hiding him on Eighteenth Street, among the people he robbed, because the color line that kept him comfortable downtown makes any white stranger the most conspicuous man in the neighbourhood. The protection is the injustice turned inside out, and it costs the people giving it something real. Let the third floor decide.

The federal case, left to itself, falls on the wrong people. The easiest convictions in the book are the Black floater drivers and precinct captains, and the Monitor's headline, fed by the machine, blames Eighteenth Street for a robbery committed against it. The party's job in the end is not to find the truth (they have it) but to make it land on the right people.

Big Sid keeps his bargains. If the party sells him the book, he pays, and nothing happens to them, and the machine is untouched, and the dead stay on the rolls. It is a real option and the campaign should not punish it with a trick, only with what it means.
Strode asks for the names of the dead to be struck. It is not redemption, and nobody on Eighteenth Street owes him forgiveness. It is the one decent thing he can still do, and it is useful.

History: the city's machine politics were in fact brought down over the following years, slowly, through the federal courts and a great many witnesses who had been small men in the machine. The campaign need not say how; only whether this book, and these people, were part of it.
dmTips: This scenario is about choices more than clues. Budget an hour for Act 1, an hour for Act 2 and up to two hours for Act 3, most of it the courtroom, the night of the snow, and the decision on Saturday.

Let every party with a claim on the book make a good case: Merriwether (justice, and convictions), Quarterman (protect Eighteenth Street from a government that has never protected it), Kearns (print everything), Big Sid (go home rich). Each is partly right. Do not tell the players which is right.

The color line turns in this scenario: the Muehlebach's Black staff know everything because no one ever asks them; Eighteenth Street can see a white stranger coming a block away. Use it. Let the players see that the people the city ignores are the ones who know it best.

Brumley is the most dangerous single enemy in the campaign: use The Professional at full strength, and remember he adapts. If the party is battered, let Voyles and Kreutz arrive at the same moment and get in Brumley's way, or let the third floor (forty musicians, Lucky Bowden, a chair, a fire hose) turn the corridor into somewhere no professional wants to be.

Do not let the ending be a lecture. The register coming out of Mr. Dandridge's window, and Lavinia's line in Jules's breast pocket, and the band playing 'Woodland Avenue' on Saturday night, should say it.
If Jules died in bn-scenario-002, Geneva receives Lavinia's line from Mr. Dandridge instead, and she sings 'Woodland Avenue' with somebody else at the piano. Do not soften it.

If the party sold the book to Big Sid, end the campaign on Saturday night at the Gold Leaf all the same, with the band, and let Heat sit at 3 for ever. Some of the band will not look at them. Geneva will; she has decided she understands, and that is worse.

Period texture: the first snow; Armistice Day posters going up for next Wednesday; the radio back to dance bands; Union Station's clock; the Muehlebach's maroon-and-gold uniforms; Christmas windows being dressed on Petticoat Lane; the new City Hall almost finished.

Experience: the 4500 XP in this file is per character and is the campaign's last award; it does not reach 7th level. A party that wishes to continue in Kansas City has a second book, Norbert's, in a safe on Main Street.
